This motion is denied in its entirety. Not to say that some of these matters are fit to be explored during cross-examination. The reasons will follow. Are there any other procedural matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Kehoe, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you like me to raise my hand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not necessary but you are free to do so if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's it? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated, Mr. Jones. Mr. Jones, you will first be examined by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, can you state your name for the record and spell your last name?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Anthony R. Jones, Anthony Ray Jones. J-o-n-e-s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, General, you are a retired military officer. Can you give us your rank when you retired from the United States army and when you refired?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I was lieutenant-general, and I retired in the end of June 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I take it from your statement that it's after 36 years of military service and over ten years as a senior military officer?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could bring up 65 ter 1D2779. Mr. President, this is Lieutenant-General Jones's report. I have also for the ease of moving through this more quickly, put a binder together of hard copies of these documents. With Your Honours' permission if I could give them to Lieutenant-General Jones at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, what is on the screen is in tab 1 of your binder. Do you recognise this as your report, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can move to page 18 in e-court, which is your resume, General, or curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not sure I understood. Tab 18?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 18 of the same document, which is your resume.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is also on the screen in front of you, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: My pages are not numbered, so bear with me a second, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you recognise that as your resume, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I would like to go to page 2 of that document which details your work experience.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, General, we're not going to go through your background in detail because the Prosecution has not objected to your expertise, but I would like to just -- can you give the Trial Chamber a brief view of your experience on a tactical, operation, and strategic levels through your career that enabled you to render an opinion not only here but previously on the roles and duties of operational commanders?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Sure. Basically I had 36 years of service starting out in the infantry. I commanded for over eight years of my tenure, I had command both in peacetime and in combat. Battalion, brigade levels. I had a wealth of experience both at the tactical level and in the Pentagon, and particularly strategic level. Recognised at my operational experience to include overseas assignments to include Bosnia, the Middle East, and other places. I was positioned as the commander of the aviation war fighting centre. I also then later on after being the Chief of Staff of the US Army Europe was returned to training and doctrine command which was responsible for developing leaders at all levels as well as the doctrine of the US Army and it was at that time that I also was selected to do the investigation of the 5th Corps leadership and -- at Abu Ghraib. So through the course of my experience, not only in operational units but in the training and doctrine command, I had an opportunity to witness leadership at all echelons, and I feel that that positions me, based on leadership that I have seen and experienced, to comment on this particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I probably should have mentioned to this to you at the outset, but to the extent that I delay in responding to you at the end of your answers it's because we're waiting for the translation to catch up.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Oh, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. General, I would just like to focus on one comment that you made on your assessment of the situation in Abu Ghraib. Can you explain that a little bit and explain to the Trial Chamber if your focus was on command -- operational commander issues at that time.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: That's basically correct. I was selected because I was senior in the time to the 5th Corps commander and I was to assess not only his role as the commander in his culpability in the incidents but also that of his staff, and my role is to look at the all the orders that was given to him, his responsibilities and the actions he took which may have precluded and/or prevented what happened at Abu Ghraib. That report is classified but basically it was at the operational level of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And thereafter -- let me ask you initially. What rank were you when you conducted this investigation and when was?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I was a lieutenant-general, and I belive that was in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And thereafter, General, were you called upon to give testimony in various locales concerning your assessment of -- I believe it was General Sanchez and his actions as an operational commander?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it was General Sanchez and his staff. That was 5th Corps combined to the -- combined joint task force 7. Following our investigation and our travel and interviews, numerous interviews, we compiled a report and then we went and we had to back brief not only the department army leadership but also the -- the office of the secretary of Defence, then we briefed the intel select committees of the president, followed by Congress and Senate, various committees to include intelligence and/or the armed services committees, both Senate and the House. Followed by that we did obviously the press releases and/or the editorial boards of prominent newspapers both international and national in the US. We submitted our report and then following that we also had to respond to inquiries and questions about that report where we could. I will try to speak slower. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would certainly help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. I just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last question in this area, General. As you're moving through the various chains of commands during your 36 years and your experience as a senior officer for the past ten year, can you give the Trial Chamber an idea of your different perspectives that you were exposed to when you became aware of, through your various posts throughout the world that enabled you to assess, not only in the case of General Sanchez but here in the case of General Gotovina, what it means to be an operational commander and what that individual's faced with and what he exactly has to do during the course of his command.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I would say I was fortunate because starting out in the infantry and then later going to other combat arms and branches I had the opportunity to see firsthand at the tactical level being deployed to different -- different theatres, and early on the opportunity to see what the effects are of an untrained force. Obviously it was 1970s when I started in the army. At that time our army was not that good and so we had to work on the training, we had to work on the non-commissioned officer corps and the junior officer leadership because that had to be the foundation of our army for the future. So I saw that firsthand. As I progressed up and had the opportunity to command soldiers, I saw very quickly the importance of leadership at the lower level as well as at the senior level and the ability and the clear guidance and how important that was. I learned how to take mission-type orders and how to understand commander's intent and what -- what the ramification were at all levels and all echelons of command. As I progressed and saw that firsthand in combat, I realised, not only in the period there in the late 1980s when I was in special operations, the importance of training, the importance of leadership, the importance of getting the whole team to focus and -- and the indispensable requirement for discipline within the ranks and each individual doing their own individual -- or upholding their own individual responsibilities. I then moved and used those lessons later on as I commanded a brigade level and then had the opportunity a couple of times to work in the Pentagon where I saw the formulation of national strategies and how the selection of courses of actions and pushing those out to the combatant commanders become very important from a strategic level. I then came in the middle 1990s, 1997, had the opportunity to serve in Bosnia where I saw even more the international committee -- community and other armies and how they approached the leadership training and in some cases lack of the non-commissioned officer corps and impact on the readiness and ability of their forces to perform. Given those experiences obviously I was selected to go back and be the commander of the Fort Barker [phoen] in the army aviation centre, the war fighting centre for all of army aviation. And I tried to impart at that time to all levels and echelons of leadership the importance of discipline, the importance of training, and being able to focus on the key and important parts to do their mission. I talked to them about experiences in combat and how leadership makes a difference. I talked to them about the discipline within the ranks and being able to teach their -- the lower level units and those leaders how to perform when they really needed to focus. Following that command tour, I returned once again to Europe. There I was selected to be the Chief of Staff of the US Army Europe. Certainly operation and strategic level for the army command component of the European command. There we had the opportunity to interface with many armies, mostly land-based armies, land-based forces, from all across Europe and former Eastern Europe. And there I witnessed also first hand as we trained with them maybe some of their voids and the experiences they needed. I was deployed several times to war training exercises, such as in Poland, to oversee operations in Kosovo and obviously back into Bosnian and those areas to help guide it and mentor some of the leadership we had. So that wealth of experience then also led me to be selected to return to be part of the army's training and doctrine command where we used and have used over time our experiences to formulate our doctrine which will lead our forces to the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jones --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you take a breath now and then the interpreters will have an opportunity to do so as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure it will work out in the future. I'm just so familiar. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see if they're caught up. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: So it was the selection, then returning to the training and doctrine of command. Based on my operational experience and observing leadership at all levels, I was able then to impart what knowledge I had and help formulate and develop the doctrine for our army, also to formulate the training regiment of which leaders at all echelons were then trained from their initial basic training all the way through senior leader experiences to include the non-commissioned officer corps. I trust that that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It does, sir. General, I just would like to shift topics now to the actual preparation of the report that you submitted to the Trial Chamber. And the first item -- obviously we looked at the report, but if could you turn to tab 2 in your binder, which is 65 ter 1D2944, a letter dated -- I'm going to do this via Sanction, a letter dated 20 May 2009.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes, have I it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, General, if can you just page through this and go to the next page and there is an appendix to this letter. Go to the third page, if we can. And then the next page. As the assumed facts, do you recognise this document, General?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you use this document in the preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I did. First of all, I looked at what was asked of me to do in terms of explaining the role of the operational commander, particularly as we -- as related to General Gotovina. And then I looked at the facts and utilised these facts as well as going back into the documents were later provided to me to read there depth. First of all, the condition of the Croatian forces, the history leading up to Operational [sic] Storm, and then what actually happened during the course of events. I looked particularly at the task organisation, the forces that were given to General Gotovina, the level of training. I also, because of the operational level, looked at how the force got to the readiness level they were or the lack of readiness level and what I thought the risk would be in any operations which the Croatian leadership had given to its commanders. That was the level which I was used to. The -- then I read, looked specifically at the orders. I looked at specific tasks and implied tasks that were given to the command, and then I looked at how, and probably the -- the strategies that were to be used to achieve those missions. I don't know if you want me to elaborate on what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will get to that in one moment, but before we do that, General --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Certainly I used this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2944.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1632 [Realtime transcript read in error "D1062"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And then if we could just flip back to tab 1, which is your report, 65 ter 1D2779.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just going to wait until it comes up on the screen. And, General, I think you just said that you used this information in this letter and the appendix as well as other documents in formulating your expert report that's on the screen and is in tab 1 of your book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2779, the expert witness report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1633.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1633 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just going back to the previous exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the number which appears on the transcript is D1062 should be D1662. That's, Mr. Waespi, I take it you wanted to raise. That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now to add to the confusion. I gave a wrong number. It's D1632 followed by the expert report, which is now D1633. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, if we can back up before we actually go into the substance of your report, and if we can look at paragraph 4 where you talk about the use of the military power being the last resort. And in paragraph 6, you talk about the level of expertise, training, and logistical capabilities of the HV. If you can, General, as a operational commander prior to this series of actions that ultimately culminated in Storm, Maestral, an Operation Southern Movement, as an operational commander, General, can you give the Trial Chamber an idea of what General Gotovina was facing and what his thought processes would have been with this type of assignment?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Sure. As I reviewed the documents, obviously I saw that we had a very young army, and I saw that it was the intent of the president of Croatia to use his military obviously as the element of a combat power after all things either diplomatic and political actions had evidently not been successful. When I looked at that as being with my background, I wanted to see, because I knew that Croatia had a young fledgling -- what force would be assigned to prosecute this offensive campaign given that Croatia had never, as far as I knew, executed an offensive campaign, and prior to this operation were basically a defensive homeland defence-type force. So as I looked at that, I looked to see what training schools, what they were doing to train their force. I looked at how they had requested assistance, trying to establish a corps curriculum for non-commissioned officers and for junior leaders which would be obviously essential if you were going to conduct this type of operation. It was apparent to me that they had a very short time to prepare for this. You cannot build a professional army in a period of three to four years. So there was an issue there which later I saw would be a risk to the total operation. I looked at it in terms of the commanders selected and how they had determined the sectors of operation, and then I looked specifically who they had given responsibilities for, which pieces of the operation, and I saw and looked at the task organisation General Gotovina was given; and I tried to track that back to who was trained, who was not trained, which forces he, in my estimate, he would be relying upon to do the main effort. As I looked at that, I did see that General Gotovina also recognised early on that he had did not have a professional force. He did not have the leadership at the junior levels, not only in officers, but he certainly didn't have it in terms of the non-commissioned officer corps, so he was going to have a very risky operation. I did see efforts from him early on, as early as 1992, where he tried to emphasise that point and tried to get training opportunities in terms of formal schooling as they formulated their -- their army. I saw few opportunities certainly because of time, as we may have done it, to do more collective training at battalion brigade regimental level to actually manoeuvre and see the forces manoeuvre, so his preparation was constrained not only by formal schooling opportunities for his leaders and individuals but also from the capability to do collective-type unit training to prepare them for this operation. So as I looked at that I obviously envisioned, and then I saw, as I envisioned, that there was a lot of risk taken by the main Croatian staff as well as the leadership to employ their military. So this obviously put a lot of responsibility and a lot of burden on commanders across the sectors, and in particular to the main effort which was General Gotovina. So, that -- that was a very critical period leading up to the selection by the -- President Tudjman and the country of Croatia to task their commanders and their military to conduct an operation which they had not heretofore done before and that put a lot of burden on the commanders on leadership to execute this mission. So it was leading up to the prosecution of the war and the campaign. I could see early on that this was going do take dedicated leadership and dedicated focus, and it would take, even then, some very specific orders, such that at all levels they would understand the intent of the operation and than then caused me to look at the orders, knowing the task organisation. Did that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It did, sir. If I can just ask a question based on one of the comments that you made, and you refer to it just briefly in your statement in paragraph 9 as well. And that is your distinction between being on the defensive and going on the offensive, which you see in paragraph 9. You say, "Offensive operations are normally the most complex operations to execute." Can you give the Chamber, given the fact that you stated we're now moving from the defensive to the offensive, can you just give the Chamber an idea of what type of transition is necessary there and frankly why is it more complex to execute.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Well, the basic tenants which make it more complicated, you have more dynamic components, more units moving. You have to control the sectors of fires. You have to have good communications to be able to track and see the battlefield. At the same time, you're looking, especially an operational commander, you have got to look and anticipate what's going on 48 hours, 72 hours ahead of you and anticipate the reaction of the enemy forces. As you move forward and either achieve success or do not achieve success, you have to arrange the priorities of your subordinate units in terms of fires, in terms of a logistic support, in terms of communications, and you have to have your intelligence really focussed so you can -- the help you enable -- help enable you to see the battlefield. So, this -- when everything is moving versus sitting in a defensive posture which you have people basically stationary, everything becomes very more dynamic and you have then more cause to change your orders while on the move, and that -- for someone that is not trained to do that, it becomes very -- I don't say risky but I would say very complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But with the logical conclusion to that be that being on the offensive puts yet more responsibility and burden on the operational commander, in this instances, General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Not only on the operational commander but all his support elements, also to include the logistics, and moving that forward, clearing the routes and also the dynamics of what the enemy is going to do because once you get through the first line of defence, there's certainly a lot of unknowns because you don't see the enemy's playbook and he has a vote in some of the operations, so you have to be able to react. You have to keep some level of reserve so that you can counter any movement by the enemy to counter your initial assault. So there is certainly many more variables in play. I would also say when you start doing something like this, you may have a very good plan but that plan is subject to change based on what happens on the battlefield, and you must continually adjust. That relationship you have with subordinate leaders and them being able to understand your orders and your intent and fulfil that also becomes very important, and it is only through training and those relationships you build over time do you develop the trust and confidence in your subordinate leaders to be able to prosecute the way that you would expect them to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, General, and I just want to follow up one of the comments you made and this is, Mr. President, on page 14, line 24. And you said that: "I envisioned there was a lot of risk taken by the Croatian Main Staff as well as the leadership to employ their military so there are obviously -- put a lot of responsibility and a lot of burden on commanders across the sectors and in particular the main effort which was General Gotovina." Now given this lack of training that you're talking about, how did that translate into a risk for General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Well, he had a combination of some forces he was able to spend some time with, I think particularly the 4th Regiment and some other battalion elements, and witnessed their training. He tried to infuse them with some of the non-commissioned officers trained in the academies and officers but certainly far less than his requirement to fulfil those positions. So, he knew, I'm sure he knew, I can't speak for him, but I would have known that I went into this -- this fight with a force that was less -- had conducted less training than I would have wished them to do. Now most commanders would say you never get enough training. But he knew that he had elements he could count on and elements he could not count on. He had also, what I would call, a high level of conscripts in his organisation, his task organisation, that apparently forced him in to do the -- to develop the plan and the strategic he did which was an economy of force in some areas and then knowing also he was probably outgunned and had less combat systems than the force he was going up against. He had the priority -- or prioritise the resources he had to be successful. So he knew he had a risky operation. He knew -- probably he knew which commanders he could reply on, which units he could rely on, and he had to manage those very carefully. He had to give the priority of support to the units he knew had to lead the effort, and I think on several times he emphasised the -- the issue of discipline in his ranks, and knowing he didn't have professional force, he probably knew that was also a risk. So, when this happens, leadership is paramount. At the point in time of the main attack or when a decision must be made at a critical point in time in the fight, that's when leadership makes a difference, and he, no doubt, realised that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, with regard to this campaign, and I just -- for reference in paragraph 40, you note that there were various operations of the offensive campaign that took place before and after Operation Storm. Is it -- my first question is: Is it important to look at, for instance, Operation Storm in the context of the overall campaign that is under way and why is it important? And why is it important to -- in viewing the operational commander's actions.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: If you go back to the mission that was given to the Croatian Army in the first place, that set the stage because there were strategic objectives at stake and so, as you went into a campaign to support those strategic objectives, a commander can't lose sight of the ultimate goal. So, as -- there's -- there's some goodness in that series of -- of -- of engagement such as, you know, Operation Winter 94, Jump 1, he, at that time, those experiences gained by those forces were building his force as -- on the move. So he knew that there was none of those individual objectives were culminating points for this offensive campaign. He had to stay focussed to the original mission given to him by the Main Staff and the country, which was to re-establish the Croatian country and/or to defeat the occupation forces. So you can -- you know, you cannot sit back on each one of those preliminary or intermediate [Realtime transcript read in error "immediate"] objectives and think that you have achieved the end. You had to stay focussed on the end state and what you were asked to do. That is something that lower levels of command usefully don't understand. They are seeing the tactical objective. So it's at the operational level you must stay focussed on what your country has tasked you to do. That is -- very few people see that when it comes to fighting the fight, because they get oftentimes too wrapped up in the task at hand, and you must continue to reiterate and focus them to the future. In that case, the operational commander must be looking for 48, 72 hours out. What's the next mission? What could happen with my forces now? What are my vulnerabilities? What is my priority which I have to redistribute my resources to make sure that I'm achieving my ultimate objective?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as -- as part of that, General, and that focus, that focus of looking ahead, is your assessment that that focus also include the movement into Bosnia-Herzegovina and Operation Maestral and Operation Southern Move?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: No doubt. I would -- I think that Operation Storm was just an intermediate [Realtime transcript read in error "immediate"] objective in the course of events of an offensive campaign, in this case which was leading to the strategic objectives. After the agreement signed with the Bosnian forces by the Croatian government, there was no doubt that that mission was going to continue with the pressure on the Bihac pocket in the north. Something had to be done in conjunction with the time of the Bosnian 5th Corps to continue that operation. I know that there was a decision to go into a defensive posture at one time, but that defence posture would have - if you didn't continue the momentum - probably would have not enabled success because your forces, when you achieve that momentum, would have probably set back and you would have not been able to achieve strategic objectives. I know that speaks very broadly. But what General Gotovina was saddled with in the main effort by his country, I don't think a lot of people realise the significance. If he didn't succeed, his country was at risk, as was the future disposition of the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would like to get a little bit more specific, General, on the fight within the borders of the Republic of Croatia as opposed to the next set -- the next movement of the campaign, be it Maestral or Southern Move. And in paragraph 8 you know that the Operation Storm was fought virtually all within the internationally recognised territory of the Republic of Croatia. In your analysis of the situation, General, how did that situation, the fight within the Republic of Croatia, how was that different from the next steps, the fights into Bosnia-Herzegovina, with regard to the division of responsibilities and who was in charge of what, and do you have some basis of that in some of the documents you looked at?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed early on that, since they were still within their own territory, the orders given and the responsibilities divided for the forces, and I would -- I attribute this a lot to the fact that General Gotovina, in his forces, were charged with the -- to attack and/or achieve the objectives, that he was not given responsibility for the rear area of operations and the re-establishment of civil law and authority. To me, that probably assisted him because as he could move through the area and then have someone take over the responsibility for re-establishing the rule of law on the civil and/or to secure the rear area allowed him to focus forward on offensive campaign. Now whether that was the intent, it certainly, to me, was spelled out in the orders given to him and given to -- from down through the minister of defence, minister of the interior. That was probably a good thing because the condition and readiness of his forces relied him to focus forward continually to conduct this offensive campaign. As complex as it was, as complex as the terrain was, the fighting through minefields to achieve positional advantage with the terrain, as rugged as it was, to focus on the objectives and the manoeuvre units, I mean, you notice all the way up until objective Storm [sic] I don't think the Croatian Army would ever deployed the two brigades abreast. It was always fighting single brigades, and it's that time the change in manoeuvre and tactics, the ability to use fires in support of manoeuvre units that was creating doctrine for the -- this young Korean [sic] Army, and so he was developing, as he went, his tactics. And he had to stay focussed, and he had to ensure the units of -- were moving appropriately. I think he also recognised a lot of his plan didn't all launch off at the same time because he had approximately someone -- 250, 300 kilometres of front lines. Although Knin was a very valuable target, the rest of his force did not move probably as he would have liked it to. So there was a lot -- lot of focus. He had to do -- across his front line and as they moved, I think it was beneficial for someone else to pick up the responsibility of the rear area and re-establish it within their legal territory, re-establishing the security and the rule of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, there is a word missing on the transcript. You said he was creating doctrine for the -- this young and then you used an adjective before you used the word army, and it's my recollection that you said Korean which I had difficulties to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, Croatian. Did I say Korean? I didn't mean to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether I heard it well, but at least it's now right on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, if you can just ask one other clarification on page 19, line 18, it reads: "So you can -- you know, you cannot sit back on one of those preliminary or immediate objectives." I think that that -- I'm not sure that that was the word immediate, but I asked the Chamber if we can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the record now that you said: "So you can -- you know, you cannot sit back on each of those preliminary or immediate objectives," that's how it reads now, "and think that you have achieved the end." Does that reflect what you said or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be intermediate objective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Intermediate objectives.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes. I earlier referred to interpreters being able to take a breath now and then but transcribers may have a similar problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. My problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President I think that if we stay on the same page, line 10 -- excuse me, page 20, line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we have at this moment, Mr. Jones, is, "I would -- I think the Operation Storm was just an immediate objective." There also I take it that you wanted to uses the word intermediate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then corrected as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, just looking at your binder and talking about this responsibility for law and order in Croatia, I note that in tabs 3, 4, and 5, you review a variety of documents. For record they're D409, the 20 August 1995 diary entry of Mate Lausic; 3 August 1995, orders by the General Lausic regarding cooperation between the military police and the Ministry of Interior. And I would like to focus on the -- tab 5, which, if we can put that on the screen, that is 65 ter 1D374 which is the minutes of a closed session of the Croatian government on 4 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's 1D1374, if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As you can see, these are the minutes that I just discussed with a variety of ministers there, and I would like to turn to page 7 in the English, where Minister Jarnjak, the minister of the interior, is talking. And page 9 in the B/C/S. And, General, I would just like to -- to focus you on the comments that begin five lines -- the middle of the fifth line down, by the minister of the interior: "Because, as the army enters the area, the military police follows which secures the line, and immediately after the regular police enters the area and takes over, all those tasks that the regular police is obligated to conduct, according to the constitution and the law and those maintaining public peace and order, protection of life and property." Now those particular comments in conjunction with the other comments, did that give you the view that you just espoused about what General Gotovina's focus was meant to be, after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Well, certainly that responsibility as outlined there which they were supposed to do to re-establish within the Croatian country the -- not only the courts, the jurisdiction, the police authority, certainly the responsibility, so that -- that to me was a good thing because it allowed General Gotovina to really look at what he had ahead of him, and he was conducting an offensive campaign. The things that he had to start looking for, obviously right after Storm was what -- what is the next mission? That being an intermediate objective, so he had a lot on his mind to focus himself forward. This, in itself, allowed the responsibility for the rear area to be under the over-sighted not only the other -- the ministers here but the forces which they had the civil, military police. It appeared, you know, how well they executed that is not in discussion but they certainly had the responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 65 ter 1D1374.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1634.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I would like to -- to just go in a little bit more deeply on what you just commented about, about the next responses and the transition and the looking ahead after the attack on Operation Storm and just explain to us a little bit the next sequence of responses, the short responses immediately after Operation Storm, what those concerns were, and then after those concerns were addressed, what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Well, if you remember, as I think about Operation Storm, the -- obviously the Main Staff had given that operation four days to prosecute which is a very short time-period. As you look at it, I also noticed with the fall of Knin, you know, I wondered at the time, and I asked the question: What was General Gotovina doing, you know, if, in fact, Knin was such a centre of focus it was a -- what I consider a key objective. However, if you think about it, the remainder of his forces across the line were not doing very well. So as it's operational commander, he had to be concerned across all his front even though he had taken risk by -- my opinion, what was an economy of force operation back in to the western part of his responsibilities, area of operation. He could get those people moving, because he become -- after Knin was taken by the 4th and the 7th there, he had to be concerned about the success of the rest of his operation, as well as the adjacent units although he been working out of Bosnia in an envelopment-type operation, he had, with the HVO forces on his right flank, he also had to be concerned about that. He did not know, probably, in my opinion, the readiness of that force. So he had now, by doing an envelopment, exposed the flank of his force, so he had to be concerned about movement of the rest of the force back-up and their success. He also had to look at his other flank and see the success of that operation, to see if it was proceeding so that he would have kind of a dual envelopment. So it became clear to me that he was probably looking at the rest of the fight knowing that Knin was being taken by his current forces. He then had to anticipate what was his vulnerabilities. As I said in my report, once an objective is taken and you learn this from your initial training, once you have taken objective, you know, if -- if you're not a professional force and trained to do this very readily, you must go quickly and posture yourself for a counter-attack from the force of which you just pushed off that objective, because that is a time which you are very vulnerable. And a lot of times a non-professional force will set back, so you must focus those people and get them prepared for potential counterattack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why are you the most vulnerable after you achieve an objective?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Because a lot of times, and in our army we saw this earlier on, going back to Vietnam days after everything, the enemy usually has anticipated your attack and probably has a reserve at some point. He's prepared now to commit that reserve against critical nodes and he would mass his forces at a point in time to counter what you just achieved. So, at the same time as you just achieved your objective, at lot of times your artillery is moving, repositioning, your forces are repositioning; and your command and control is not as good as it was because people have a tendency to have a letdown and go into this -- this probably -- I call it self-satisfaction that they have achieved something without being able to look ahead but they have to stay focused and leadership must keep them focuses in going forward. That's the difficulties in an offensive campaign versus defensive campaign. Defensive, you may have kicked the force back, you're still in the same position. You get some re-arm, refuel, but now you're moving and you're on terrain that you didn't heretofore hold and you're not familiar with it, so you have to keep focussed and keep moving. The enemy has been on that terrain. He knows that terrain and he probably knows his avenues to counter-attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to a document that -- it is in your binder as P20, and it is the war diary that you looked at, and if you can turn to page 87 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can call P71 up and 87 in the English. If we can spin that around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is talking about 5 August 1995, the day that they took Knin. And General Gotovina notes: "I am warning that the battle is still on until we carry out our deblockade." Is that consistent with what you're talking about at the time, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes, for sure. I mean, the comment there musn't be euphoria is right on. That shows you how he still sees the battlefield. He still sees the fight and you cannot develop complacency. You must continue to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, how does this looking forward then exhibit itself, for instance, in terms of setting up an active defence. What's that interplay between taking your objective, active defence and then moving ahead from there?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Sure. Well, leading up to this, if you think back from the winter of 1994 and then this movement through this very difficult terrain, commander knows that those forces that have led the main effort obviously -- not only they develop casualties, they probably have both some level of mental and physical fatigue; and he has to keep that in mind as he prepares for the next fight. So normally when would you go into an active defence, it would bring some of the forces forward to defend the lines where you gave those forces which -- who have been fighting for the last 48, 72, one week, whatever it may be, whatever the period may be, to give them a little bit of rest, an ability to regroup, get a couple of hours of sleep before going into the next fight. At the same time, you have to enable that commander and his staff to plan the next fight and take the orders you are passing to them, re-task, organise for the next phase. So all that must happen, and it's easier to do if you go into an active defence and bring some of the reserve forces on to the line, who may be a little bit fresher, and enable them to hold that line, while you reset the forces who have just been fighting for the period. It's a calculated risk if you are able to do that and afford yourself where those units 12, 24 hours, whatever it may be, to reset before you start the next operation. And in this particular case, as I saw in the orders, he elected to take that risk rather than to continue to deplete his forces, give them an opportunity to reset and rest before he -- he -- what he saw was the next operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you also see that there was, in fact, a counter-attack several days after the active defence order was implemented on the 9th of August?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I'm not surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I want to talk a little bit about the actual planning of Operation Storm before we move into some of the other aspects of your report. And if we could just go back to your binder, and we're going to go through all these documents, but in tab 6, 7, 8, and 9, and we have a series of documents that you reviewed, the first being D956, directive from the Main Staff, HV Main Staff, 26 June 1995; D957, order for Storm to General Gotovina, 26 June 1995; D958, attachments to the order for attacking, 27 June 1995; P1125, which is the Kozjak order, dated 2 August, by General Gotovina for the offensive operations for the Split Military District. And you noted previously there was a very short period of time between the actual issuance of the attack order and the onset of Operation Storm, and if we could pull up on the screen, P1125, which would be tab 9 in your binder, General, which is the Kozjak order of 2 August 1995. And if -- if we could actually go to the next page of this document. And then one more page in, please. Now, General, you have reviewed this document, have you not?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, looking at this order and General Gotovina as an operational commander, what is the role of General Gotovina as the operational commander with respect to the planning of a major operation, such as this?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I think, as you see in this order, he has selected and task-organised the units. He's given an axis of advance by his lead elements and then he also would designate the reserve and who would follow on that main effort. So, as operational commander, he has oriented his forces towards their next objectives and the avenues and intent at which he wants them to manoeuvre. He has then aligned the supporting priorities to support the main effort as well as take into consideration what he sees or pictures the enemy disposition to be. So the operational commander, in this very short period of time -- this is almost more like a frag order than a detailed order. But now he is continuing to fight. He is orienting those forces on the axis of advance and task-organising very quickly to be able to prosecute as he sees as the next objective, and that is his role. He has to think about what could go wrong, obviously, if he is not successful. It is not as easy as just giving his regiments an orientation. What if they are not successful? What is his reserve? What is his other courses of action if he is not successful? Anticipating what the fight will be and what other orders he may have to give to ensure that they are successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, if I can just clarify one thing. I understand what you're talking about, but heretofore in this case, I don't think we've heard the terminology, "frag order." Can you explain that for me?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Usually you will have a large base order for an offensive campaign which would detail, just as we saw in the original orders, all the annexes for logistics, intelligence, communications, rear area OPs, if it pertains to them and so forth. You take that base order and then as you go through the campaign and you're given very quick orders from - as you see in this sequence - the Main Staff to continue the fight, or to change directions, you use that base element and then you order -- you publish a fragmentation order which is a piece order to supplement your original order, and it usually just re-prioritises the supporting elements, the priorities of fires, the axes and direction of advance. So you don't have to rewrite a 100-page document. You just give very concisely what's changed from the base orders, and that is generally referred to as a frag order. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, we talked about General Gotovina's role in drafting or involving himself in the attack order that we have before. What's the role of the subordinate commanders in this planning of this military operation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Okay. What he would do was give the priorities of effort, and then the subordinate commanders, if it's in their area of responsibilities, would provide a detailed plan, for example, the artillery, the fires annex. He would give priorities of fire to different categories. Then the commander -- or the chief of the fires brigades would then take those priorities and develop a detailed target list. If the logistics priority set was priority to 4th Guards Regiment, the logistics commander would then orient his supply trains to give them the priority, in terms the ammunition, water, food, whatever it may be, as supplies. So he would -- he would then dictate and approve the priorities of effort for his subordinate commanders. For his manoeuvre commanders, you saw he would give them an orientation or an axes of advance. They would figure out in detail how then to manoeuvre their forces, subordinate forces, through that area oriented on where he told them to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let's use just an example. If you can go to page 7 -- section 7 of this document, which is page 14 in the English, and I will check it on the artillery section. As is this is coming up in the B/C/S, General, you just mentioned the artillery aspect, and you said the chief of the fire brigades. I take it you mean the artillery brigade would then take those priorities and develop a detailed target list. That is at page 32, line 4 and 5. Using this information that's in -- concerning artillery support, just can you explain that in a little bit more depth. This information goes out from General Gotovina and what does the chief of artillery then do?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Okay. As you see here, the other thing he has done is task-organised the supporting artillery to re-enforce the Operations Group North by giving them more assets, so not only has he determined the priority of fires, he has told them to wait a different subordinate command with what forces he has. So he has that within obviously his purview. The -- then you see what's happening. He has told them where to orient their fires and the priorities. Now the artillery group commander must take that information and do his targeting and make sure that he has assigned different batteries and different guns, the capability to prosecute those priorities. And so he would then plan in detail the targeting, the allocation, the rounds per target, and those kind of details and which element was going to fire on those targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in General Gotovina's orders would you expect to see specific targets listed in this order, and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't object to the first point about artillery because it was fairly general. But now we going to target lists. There is nowhere in the report any mentioning of target lists, and as Mr. Kehoe pointed out, I think, last week, on Tuesday, he said that on transcript page 2887: "The opinions that this expert are going to employ are in the actual report. There is not going to be any divergence from these opinions. We are simply giving the array of documents that could potentially come up during direct examination." So this is a total new area developed now on the stand which there is no foundation also about -- documents, other documents that the witness has seen, so I object to continuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if I may, these documents, of course, were disclosed to counsel as documents that we were going to use with regard to the duties and responsibilities of an operational commander in executing a plan such as Operation Storm or any other plan, are outlined in this report. The only thing we're doing here is taking documents in evidence, digging one step down, and asking that question: As the operational commander, would you expect to see these specific targets set forth in this order? That's all it is. It's just an extension of what the duties and responsibilities were of an operational commander as opposed to his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would leave it to that one question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Back to your question, I would not expect to see the target list in General Gotovina's orders. I would expect to see a detailed target list down in subordinate orders, of which, you know, they would take the intelligence and then apply the target list and coordinates and what weapons system would fire on those. So, no, I would not expect that at the operational level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you mentioned previously matters like logistics and communications. Would you likewise expect more detailed orders at the more subordinate level outlining exactly how logistics were going to be taking care of communications?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I would. I would also -- I would expect in the operational order level to re-establish the priority of support, based on the changes and task organisation. I would also -- that priority support may also dictate things like priority of air support, priority of intelligence, and other things, which could enable the success of the main effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: A couple of more questions on the beginning of a -- of a separate topic, Mr. President. I think we do some preliminaries before we move into the meat of it because I note we have five minutes more, so if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'd like to shift gears, if we may, and talk about items that you discuss in paragraphs 19 and 28 of your report, and it has to do with the command climate and you note that the commander - this is in paragraph 19 - establishes the culture and command climate within his subordinate units. And in paragraph 28, you elaborate on that just a bit more. Talk a little bit about the command climates and how would an operational commander such as General Gotovina convey the command climate. What would he do on a general level and a more specific level? How is it done, General?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Well, it starts with training. When the commanders is assigned to a unit, obviously the units ask themselves, Can I trust this leader? So he has got to -- by his actions, his words, his emphasis on key elements, he has got to set the conditions of: Who am I, what's important, and what are my expectations by leaders at all echelons? He does that not by sitting behind and writing documents to -- professes that. He does that by his presence at key places, such as key training events. He does that by holding key forums of his leadership, to really make sure that they understand what his intent is, by his actions, what he does or fails to do is observed by his subordinate leaders. So -- and it also -- by being at key events which dictates that leadership should be there, his presence makes a difference. So that's why you see, irregardless of the battlefield, but it would be training, would it be sometimes when the situation is tough, leadership must be present, must be supporting subordinate leaders but also must be able to make sure that when they're not there, they're carrying out his intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to go into a series of documents that may be easier for the Chamber to view as a whole as to opposed to breaking it up. On that score, it may be a logical time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will have a break, and we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, staying with the command climate issue, I'd like to talk to you just a bit about the element of discipline in command climate, and the reference point that'd like to take off from is the last sentence in paragraph 43 of your report where you note, based on the directives and commander's intent as propagated in the written and verbal orders, "... this type of activity" -- I'm talking about undisciplined activity, "... this type of activity was not to be condoned by the military or leadership at any level." And on that score, General, I'd like to discuss with you a series of documents, beginning with the -- again the operational diary, P71, which is tab 20 in your binder. And if we could turn to page 47 of the English, and we are focussing here, General, on the period of time just after Operation Summer 1995 in the Bosanski, Grahovo, and Glamoc area and prior to Operation Storm. What I would like to do, General, is just discuss a few series of entries here so we can move through this relatively quickly and then ask you a question based on the items that we will discuss. And the first entry as I noted is the Ademi meeting, under the entry for 1820, General Ademi, being General Gotovina's Chief of Staff. And it notes midway through that paragraph: "After command related problems in the units, looting and arson reported in the area of Glamoc and Bosanski Grahovo." I would like to turn you ahead to paragraph -- to page 49 where towards the top of the page, 72nd VP, that is the 72nd Military Police Battalion, warning that last night about setting fires in houses. We move ahead to paragraph -- excuse me, page 56 in the English, and this is an entry on 29 July 1995 -- excuse me, 30 July 1995. In the middle of that page, General Gotovina said: "It is required to prevent arson," and the rest. And the rest. And the bottom of that is illegible. Again, moving ahead to page 62 in the English for an entry on the 31st of July, this is an entry by the 72nd military police -- it's brigade but ... Towards the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can I scroll that down a little bit in the English, and we'll just wait for it to come up in B/C/S. I understand we're just going to work with the English. It notes that the military police say that the phenomenon of arson in Grahovo is under control. The last two entries are on the 1st of August and there are in fact two entries, the first being on page 69 at a meeting on the 1st of August of 1995, midway through that entry for General Gotovina: "The biggest problem in OG Sjever, which is OG North, is the lack of discipline, so we ordered to the commanders of the units to pay attention and strictly forbid looting and burning." If I may, just round that particular day out, if we can go up to page 73, if we can spin that towards the left hand column, where Minister Susak, the Minister of Defence is at the bottom of the left-hand side page saying: "Past Glamoc and Grahovo. Very disappointed by burning and looting. Especially noticeable in the 4th and 7th Guards Brigade." The evidence that we've had to date, General, as we discussed outside the Court was that the 4th and the 7th was part of OG North or OG Sjever. Now, likewise - and this is on the 1st of August - but I would also like address with you some of the planning documents for Operation Storm and turn to D201, which is tab 10 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you're going at a high speed. The Susak entry is for what date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's for the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, oh yes. You said two entries are on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now tab 10 are operational orders for Kozjak 95. And if we can turn to page 2 and 3 of this document, focussing on the items 5, 6, and then 8. 5 being familiarise members with conduct and occupied settlements and handling of war booty. 6 being familiarizing units with the need to eliminate all negative occurrences that will surface in the course of combat operations with a focus on preventing torching and destruction of larger populated areas and towns. Moving down to item 8, advising members of units on conduct with civilians and POWs, in accordance with the Geneva Convention. Lastly before I move into the questions, I would like to turn our attention to D793, which is tab 11 in your book. We have the order of 1 August 1995 -- excuse me, 3 August, 1995, I apologise; I was looking at a different item. Of 3 August 1995 in keeping with the order for attack of the commander of the Split Military District, giving the reference numbers, and with the purpose of having a uniform command and control of the units ... Staff Rahim Ademi -- "Staff Brigadier Rahim Ademi is temporarily appointed commander of OG North. He shall perform the said duty alongside his establishment duty. The outgoing commander of OG North, Colonel Slave Zdilar, is to resume his duty as acting chief of infantry at the Split forward command: "This order shall come into effect immediately." Signed General Gotovina. Now, General, prior to coming in to day you have reviewed all these documents, have you not?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber your analysis culminating in this change of command for OG North less than 24 hours from -- from the beginning of Operation Storm, and how it plays into your conclusions in paragraph 43 about conduct, improper conduct not being condoned.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: If you think about it, what's going on here from an operational commander's standpoint, the questions you have to ask yourself: What were the rules set in place before operations started. And a good example is your Exhibit 10 where you talk -- where the orders talk about preparations prior to operations, during operations and post-operations. So, clearly, this annex in itself talked to the fact of reiterating and re-emphasising the important of not only control of civilians but disciplined behaviour. The second part of that also talked about during the execution of not condoning it, and the third part then talked to assisting with the stabilisation and post-combat activities. That is a normal sequence. So in the course of the events the documented orders obviously outline what the expectations and the commander's intent was. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue, you're referring to your exhibit number 10?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the one just in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I think -- are you referring to the tab numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, that's a tab number, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: D201 is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies, D201.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, the work got put on the left part of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D201, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says preparation for combat, and then the second sequence is in the course of combat operations, and the third and from a -- the way I look at that is a sequence of events of expectations. So clearly the commander's intent was outlined. Now, no doubt, as I looked at the different exhibits burning and looting was happening and had happened and this was in the period before Storm. From the operational commander's standpoint, the question arises, did he communicate to his subordinate leaders his expectations, and, of course, as a professional force, a commander is always concerned about disciplined behaviour and to see indisciplined behaviour is no doubt disappointing. So, as you look at that from the operational level, you have to think in terms of everything else that's going on, was this a trend, was this a pattern, was it focussed in certain units, and what was being done about it. And it appears, leading up the events where the commander of Operational Group north was replaced, it obviously appears to me that, in that particular organisation -- or the subordinate units of that organisation were not executing the commander's intent. And this was a very critical period. This was on the eve almost of Operation Storm, so to take actions to replace the commander, the Operational Group commander, on the eve of the next fight, tells me that obviously the trust and confidence in that commander was no longer there to prosecute the orders or his ability to lead his subordinate elements and get the right discipline and execution that was demanded. You know, you think about this at the time. General Gotovina didn't have a lot of resources to replace commanders with, and this is one of his -- his direct reports, as he has established the four Operational Groups at this time. So it's a significant event to replace one of those four, sending back to Split to which -- in my -- my interpretation is the school house in the rear, and then take his Chief of Staff and put him in charge of that group. So, to me, he obviously, though I can't -- wasn't -- I can't speak for him, was disappointed in the effectiveness of that leader and therefore he replaced him, even though he knew it was the eve of the next major fight. So that was a significant event for the total force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, would you allow me to seek some clarification. You're giving an interpretation of why you think this order to replace, let me just, for argument's sake let me give you an alternative. Colonel Slave Zdilar had reported that he was not in a very good physical condition, suffering from kidney stones or whatever, and had reported that he might have difficulties in performing his task. I mean, that's an alternative possibility. What makes your alternative stronger than mine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my focus is on prosecuting the war. There's no doubt to me there's -- at this time after fighting for 18 months, numerous commanders had either mental or physical problems they had to deal with. That comes with, you know, personal courage and being able to step up and -- because this is a very critical time in this offensive campaign. My -- and, of course, did I not read anything that showed me that was a -- was a consideration, but it appeared to me, as any commander would be, there was a series of indisciplined behaviour in some units of which General Gotovina was relying on to be his main effort, and he was not going to tolerate that, nor would have I, and obviously his -- the person next to him who was responsible was not carrying out his orders or his intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have understood your explanation. That's not my problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My problem would be, how does that appear from this document? I mean, the document saying something about uniformed command and control of the units but not giving any further details. What -- I mean, you are linking more or less the -- and that's what we talked about, indisciplinary behaviour with perhaps what happens here, and -- now, I'm trying to find out where in this document that link is supported by the language of this document, apart from I can see that if the situation was, as you think it was, then it's quite logic to do what you have done here. But I'm asking myself: Could there be other situation in which it would be as logic to take a similar action.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if it was -- well, we're hypothesizing a little bit here, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We or I or you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, what you just proposed to me was an alternative way of looking at this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And of course, I'm asking myself to what extent --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE ORIE -- your explanation is hypothetical as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's, of course, the issue I'm raising.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would suggest to you that not only the series has documented incidents of behaviour or indiscipline within the units was a -- a good indication of the effectiveness of this commander to take the orders and/or the intent of the commander and pass those to his subordinate leaders. So, the trust that General Gotovina had probably most likely in this commander to command and control his elements and/or to garner the trust and confidence of them in his decision authorities was probably in doubt, and therefore he wanted to make sure that someone was in charge who he had the trust and confidence to prosecute the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with that document, General, in the prefatory language, does the comment "with the purpose of having a uniformed command and control of the units," if you see that on the screen. It's on the screen right now, the document we just looked at. In keeping with order for a -- the attack order of the commander of the Split Military District with the purpose -- and with the purpose of having a uniformed command and control of the units, you find -- did you find that particular comment of some significance in coming to your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's a documented way of saying, I've lost the trust and confidence in a subordinate leader, and I want someone who will prosecute my direction, my orders, and my intent, which allows you to have that uniformity of command all the way down through all echelons and that's what he was after, to make sure that his guidance and direction was not only getting to his immediate commanders or sub-commanders but also down to the lowest levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, under these circumstances, on the eve of Operation Storm, and being confronted with allegations of looting and burning by -- the 4th and 7th were part of Operative Group North, and the removal of this commander on the eve of Operation Storm, literally less than 24 hours, putting yourself in the position of General Gotovina as an operational commander would have you done anything else, to set this control climate or the --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Command climate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Command climate, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Had I been in that position, and I had seen the events leading up to me that would -- we would -- it necessitated me to take that action, first of all I would regret that I would have to do that as I entered into combat the next day. But, clearly, it showed that he had the courage to do it, because he did not have the faith in that commander to lead his soldiers into a fight, so he took that burden on his shoulders to take the risk, relieve the commander, and then put one of his own people into that position and therefore he had to go without a Chief of Staff obviously for the fight, that was a -- a courageous move as far as keeping, you know, his command team intact a -- a destructive move but obviously something he seen that had to happen. Now, once he did that, he must move on. The fight's the next day. So I think that sent a signal to subordinate commanders that he did not tolerate indisciplined activities, but, at the same time, he expected his subordinate commanders to -- to prosecute his intent as well as his orders, and he had to put that behind him and focus on the fight, because the next day, they -- he and all his forces were entering into objective Storm and that mission. So, at that time, I don't see anything else he would need to do, because he just sent a strong signal that someone who had been with him and he had appointed him to a position, he's now relived him of his duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The first part was the responsive if he was asked whether he would have done anything else, and then he mentioned into -- again his assessment of what he thought General Gotovina did. But I think the last sentence cleared it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So to conclude this, General, as an operational commander in reviewing the sequence of events prior to Operation Storm but after Summer 95 and the events in Grahovo and Glamoc, do you believe that General Gotovina took all necessary and reasonable measures to address these discipline problems?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: At that point in time, yes. I think you will see later that he followed up with re-emphasising the points as he continued operations that he was not going to tolerate and he needed some help in creating the law and order needed in the rear areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can move on to another aspect of the command climate in addition to the items that we just talked about in D201 and D793. And on the subject of NCOs, which you talk about to some degree in paragraph 25 of your statement, and the effectiveness or non-effectiveness of non-commissioned officers - I'll give you a second to get to that - now without going into this in detail you do speak about the necessity of effective -- non-commissioned officer leadership at a small unit level and how important that is. And I would like to -- to talk with you just about one exhibit that you've reviewed, and it's in tab 12 of your binder, which is D1596. General, I think this is the document you alluded to previously from February of 1995, but we'll bring it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, you have seen this document before you came here today, did you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can go to the seconds page of this document, and, of course, we're not going to read it. But when you read this document and the concerns that General Gotovina expressed to the Ministry of Defence, the Main Staff, tell us what you took from this document in assessing where General Gotovina was vis-a-vis the -- not only his operational commander responsibilities but what kind of issues and problems he was facing. And this is the document talking about NCOs and the shortage of NCOs, et cetera, and training.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: No doubt, at this time, and if you think back, General Gotovina just finished the winter campaign, and he was looking ahead to prosecute -- or continuing the offence. He realised that as he had saw prior, in the years prior, that the Croatian Army did not have a competent professional force, particularly in non-commissioned officers and junior officer leadership.
