And this point here we -- as I looked at this, reinforced the fact that not only were they not training or had a sufficient training programme that was producing non-commissioned officers or junior officers quick enough to support their needs, he was using an example, the current status of his forces, and the subordinate forces in the subordinate forces in these functional areas, not only the infantrymen and so forth but in the communications, the logistics, and the other areas of transporters, show what their shortages were on the eve of continued operations. So he was re-emphasising to the leadership of the main support staff and the ministers, ministers of defence, the need to build this capability within their army, if they were going have a professional force. Now, the results of this obviously was a field commander speaking to the highest levels to resource the training aspect continued to develop doctrine and provide me the resources I need, if you're going to give me the responsibility to fight this fight. So this was, I think, documentation from the standpoint of recognising that he did not have the junior leadership that he needed with the tasks he saw ahead of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again in paragraph 25, you talk about the need for effective non-commissioned officers as a part of team-building and growing together as a unit. How important is that trained NCO corps when it comes to executing orders concerning discipline of those lower level troops?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it's essential. If you think about it, as you -- you know, you got General Gotovina up here at the operational command level. The ones who were actually conducting the small unit tactics, manoeuvring individuals on the battlefield or the non-commissioned officers and the young officers. So the direct contact with those people and how they are trained, how they react to the orders and fight and execute their mission is a direct result of the ability of that team which has been built by the non-commissioned officer to do that. Likewise, it's that person at the point of the spear who would ensure that discipline is within the team and that each individual is doing his or her individual responsibilities. That's how you build a team, and you discipline that team to execute in accordance to the orders given you. So, at the point of the spear, so to speak, that is the people who are executing the plan at the lowest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I take it -- the logical conclusion that without that proper training, that executing of discipline would be compromised?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Initially you're trained at -- in the school house or in those -- as General Gotovina was telling to the minister, I need the school house producing these people who understand that, and then when you get to the unit, it's that team that's built within the unit by those junior leaders and the soldiers who work for them to execute that through the tough times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I would like to move ahead in the document and turn to -- it is P822, which is tab 13 in your binder, and it is a European Commission Monitoring Mission report for 27/28 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can bring that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we'll go on to talk about the bottom thereafter page. And looking at the military situation, this is a discussion that is chronicled, a discussion with General Gotovina that is chronicled. And towards the bottom of the page, it says: "The General expected cooperation and joint training with countries like the US, Germany, France, being countries friendly to the Croatian cause." If we can go to the next page at the top. And this is the item I would like to emphasise to you: "About lessons learned in Operation Storm both positive and negative. The latter being the lack of control with undisciplined soldiers of professional [sic] units doing extraordinary things" -- excuse me, "non-professional soldiers": "...undisciplined soldiers of non-professional units doing extraordinary things. The general stated that the HV lacked and still lack the level of skilled NCOs and medium level commanders able to control the soldiers." Now, when you looked at these two items together in conjunction with your other assessment of the military operations that were under way both prior to Storm and after that, what did you conclude, as an operational commander in General Gotovina's possession -- position both before, during, and after, concerning problems that were in existence under his command?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Well, if you think about this, this is now October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After Southern Movement.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Right. So from the initial recognition, if the Croatian Army was going to have a professional army, you needed a supporting foundation of schools to produce the junior leaders, non-commissioned officer corps, and so forth. Re-emphasised from the fact after the initial parts of the offensive campaign by General Gotovina in February reiterating the fact to the minister of defence in February. Now he has firsthand experience over a period of 15, 18 months of seeing his units, his subordinate units and listening to commanders at the lower levels talk about the need for these disciplined leaders as well as disciplined soldiers at the lowest levels. So this to me says: As I look back as the operational commander, if we want to continue for the future, we must not let this happen to our forces in the future. We must build the force now with the supporting institutional schooling and capabilities to make us a professional force. So this is a realisation, to me, of what he has seen and the recognition of those problems he initially thought he would have come to fruition and he thinks back on what had happened, he probably at the same time - and I again I can't speak for him - was recognising the fact of what they accomplished with the force he had and the lack of training and lack of probably preparation he would have liked to had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I'd like to again stay on this topic of command climate, and again going back to the paragraph 43, your last sentence concerning undisciplined behaviour not being condoned. And I'd like your assessment, General, of a -- several videos. Now you did view several videos from the 6th of August, 1995, before you came here today, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just going to play the first video if we can, General, and I'd like to give your previously assessment of that video as an operational commander. I'd like to bring up Exhibit D792.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will say for the record, Mr. President, I know it's been sometime since we have looked at this video. There are, in fact, two videos as Your Honour may have recalled. This is the initial video and then there's another video that is a continuation of this that the parties have agreed is a continuation where General Gotovina is going to the map and talking about the next level of operation. I -- I focus, Your Honour, on that so we don't have to play both of them, but just so the record is clear, there are, in fact, two. And I didn't want the Court to think I was just speaking of that in isolation nor have we just viewed -- have a -- given this video to -- to General Jones. The other video is -- the second video is D979, for the record. But if we could play this particular clip which is got -- I believe it's got the commentary or the translation at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "And all the rest that was tasked, the tasks that were issued lasts night and I'm not calling upon you to account for yourselves. Security services, Generalic, did he pass it on to Loza? First, did the political affairs department do its job? No, it didn't. Ceko, you were at the meeting, weren't you? Zelic was here; he had other tasks. You were at the meeting. What have you dont since last night? Was the county prefect contacted? Did you verify whether the counter prefect was contacted? Was civilian protection requested? Were the firefighters requested? "They have been requested, General. "And where are they then? Do you realise that everything has to be ready by 5.00 this afternoon, everything? Was it that difficult to find just a single cross here? A single cross. Skoric where is the cross? "We couldn't find one. It should be coming -- "You didn't find a cross, you fucking imbicile. Had you stopped in Sinj by the church there and asked the friar there to give you a cross, he'd have given you ten of those. Because you're idiots, incompetent. But you're good enough to pose in front of those cameras, those screens to be photographed. You're good enough for that. Just one example, you weren't even able to get hold of a single cross. "Let me not even begin to mention what I could see in the town. It's a disgrace. A disgrace. Barbarians and vandals act like that, those who are paid with war booty and wage war for war booty. "The unit commanders from Sinj to Knin, with the help of the engineers, have the task today to get the entire road in order. Everything, the vehicles, all that dirt, throw it out, clean it up. Clear it. The army is not to be seen in the streets. The military police is not in groups but is deployed at all check-points. They took a map of the town as planned and systematically set up check-points and is in control of the town. The military police commanders are patrolling. Patrol vehicles are patrolling the town. Cooperation with the civilian authorities in the form of the civilian police is to be established until General Cermak, who has just arrived this morning, can take over these matters and take matters into his own hands. And until then, if he is left alone, by 5.00 tonight nothing will be ready but we will have chaos again. What a disgrace. Do you realise that prime minister is coming, the ministers, the minister of transportation and all that. Everybody arriving today will enter into a town that the Croatian Army went through and which it still had under its control because the civil authorities haven't taken over yet. Who are you trying to embarrass? You are embarrassing yourself and those under your command for whom you are responsible. And all of our people who died, who were killed, you are responsible, people who gave their lives for this, you should have a little respect because people have died for the sake of Knin and all the way from Dinara since this winter, last October. Not to mentioned the recent operations and how many perished and how many are still in hospital to this very day and those maimed for life. And yet you behave like this and you call yourself commanders. Security. What is security? Security must be organised. It's in control of the situation. The military police must obey. They are the executors, the technical executors. They are the guardians of the Code of the armed forces. It guarantees the implementation and application in the field. Political affairs department. I don't see any posters in the street. No flags at any of the major facilities, installations. Nothing. Where is -- where is all of that? "Being put up, even as we speak, General. "What's being put up? Where is it? It's 11.30, since this morning, since 4.00, in fact, you should have been doing this all through the night. A helicopter is available. Everything is available to pursue this with total efficiency and yet you don't know how to make use of all of this. If you don't know how to work, do your job, something, whatever. Since nobody dragged you by your hair to become what you are, then gentlemen, go ahead and join the infantry, go into battle. You will end up saying, Well, I was -- I am a warrior. The fuck you are. Every day is a new day for a warrior and every day a warrior has to prove himself."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I thought -- Mr. Misetic is giving me bad information here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the transcript is now complete. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, just for the record, did you view yet another tape where General Gotovina is at the map shortly after this giving instructions out?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw two, this one and the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, just looking at this situation as an operational commander, how do you interpret what is going on here? What is happening, what's General Gotovina doing?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, he's obviously not pleased. If you remember, he did not come in to Knin till the day after or so forth that actually the fight had fought. He had been back looking at the overall progress of his operation, not only at that point in time but also through the other sectors, and he had seen lack of progress in the other sectors as he made his assessment. So that was on his mind and -- his -- to him, I think, in my mind, he was thinking, We have a very fragile situation. Yes, we have taken this key terrain, this key city, but there's a lot of other things that are still at risk. And if his forces didn't continue to move, then this may be short lived. At the same time, he was thinking they were also vulnerable to what the enemy would do to probably counter the action they had just done in Knin and try to retake that city. So then, as he -- he finally arrived in the town, what I saw in the video he was no doubt very disappointed in what commanders had do done to not only secure the town and continue the operation but also prepare for the defence and/or a possible counterattack, so in his mind, he had seen obviously the lack of command presence by his subordinate commanders, and that has caused him, first of all, to try to refocus them on just what the hell was going on and the importance of what was going on, and, you know, not to rest on your laurels, as I said earlier, or be complacent about taking just an intermediate objective, but preparing and continuing to prepare your soldiers in getting them focussed for the next fight, and they obviously had not done that. He used several, what I would consider, examples by the political affairs and so forth, bus those were just points to show them very vividly where they had not prosecuted their operation, turned the area over to the military police, and continued to prepare for the next fight. That was -- in my opinion, a -- they were very much at risk at that point because there was no leadership going on in the units there that had just taken Knin, and he had to get them turned around, and if he didn't, and I think you see in there, there was statement about getting the soldiers out of the town. He needed to get them out to where they needed to be not to be consumed with the euphoria of just what they accomplished and that also reinforces -- to me, he had probably as one of the few in this situation, a view of what had to happen next and the -- still the responsibility was upon him to be prepared to continue the fight, you know, given the ministers and others who were coming in to visit that afternoon and the person who was supposed to be in charge of the sector, okay, understand, but his primary concern was making sure his units and his commanders continued to follow his orders and get their soldiers moving. If they didn't they were very vulnerable at that point in time, and I think he realised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The particular venue that General Gotovina used, I mean, was that -- where he has all of his commander there, is that a venue that would have the most influence on the group as a whole?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, that's where you can very efficiently at one point in time, because if you think about it, it was not only the leadership right there in Knin there, he had the leadership across his front. He pulled them in for that period of time so they could directly hear what he had to say. When you get to an event like that, then the commander obviously has some concern. If he -- you know, if it was focussed on just these two or three commanders here, he would have grabbed those two or three commanders, but he wanted to make sure every one of his commanders heard directly from him what his expectations are. That's what I took out of that. As I looked around the room, I also -- in my case, I watched the body language of those commanders, and you could tell who -- who probably felt that they had not done what they were supposed to just by their body language. That's my experience. But he wanted to get them together because he to focus them on continuing the operation, and he could not allow complacency to set in in his ranks or his commanders at that point in time, a very critical event because he realised, I think, that he was shouldered with the burden and responsibility for the Croatian country based on the orders given him and he better be moving. That's what you face, you know, you see directly at the operational level being able to satisfy the strategic objectives, and he was probably one of the few people in that room that realised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I talked too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that realisation of the strategic objectives, as we move forward we noted that this particular video was on the 6th of August. I would like to show you a cable -- a US code cable, 65 ter 1D2934 and, General, that's tab 14 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Could I say one other thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: What I didn't address is the other part of your question was the second video. So reinforcing what I just said, I think if we'd have watched the second video, you've seen him transition with the commanders after he had, obviously vividly, told them of his disappointments and where they had failed, to get their head back in the game, and he stepped to the map and he started outlining the next operation. That's when you transition from okay -- I got your -- if I'm sitting there as a subordinate commander who says, okay, I got it, I didn't do well or we didn't do well, but then he's saying we have another fight to fight, and then he stood and started giving guidance for the next operation, that to me was very timely also, as I looked at. I'm sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. I don't know if you wanted to view that again, but --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: No, I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I'm sure you all have seen it several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We have. On that score, if we can just take a look at this cable, 6th August 1995. United States code cable. And if we could go to page 2, paragraph -- or should be point 2 or paragraph 2 of this document where it notes that: "The Croatian foreign minister, Mate Granic, told the ambassador that the government of Croatia and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina would cooperate militarily in Bosnia. Following the victory in the Krajina, the government of Croatia would 'supplement' the Bosnian 5th Corps by raising its strength from 15 to 25.000. And the 5th Corps would begin a drive towards Prijedor. Granic said that the Bosnian-Croatian militia, HVO supported by the Croatian Army, would continue military campaigns towards Drvar, Donji Vakuf, and Jajce. They would then move to push Serb artillery away from Mostar and Dubrovnik. Afterwards they will, in consultation with the international community, mainly the United States, help to open the Sarajevo corridor." Now, this is the 6th of August, General, the same day as the speech that you have. Can you interpret these two items together on a strategic level and General Gotovina's actions coming down on an operational and tactical level, given this information?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Well, my first -- my first several thoughts about this. I -- let me look at this. First of all, the game has just changed. The responsibilities have just escalated because the Croatian president has agreed obviously with the Bosnian force to join forces and move on an axis within the Bosnia-Herzegovina area. That, in effect, is a very strategic issue, and then it -- it's obvious me that probably General Gotovina had this information when he talked to his commanders and he started mapping the direction for the next operation. There's a lot of responsibilities for an operational commander now with your moving into Bosnian-Herzegovinian territory, plus you have now multiple -- on your flanks armies of the 5th Corps and/or whoever would be on your other flank, he also assumes more responsibilities for this sector even though his -- I think his sector narrowed to about a 100 kilometres, he assumed more responsibility for moving at a pace now which would be coincident with the 5th Corps which would be on his left. So this also made him the main attack for what Croatian forces would be in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he shouldered that responsibility that was given to him, and probably selected by the trust and confidence put in by Tudjman and others in his leadership. So increase in responsibility, continue the fight, your offensive campaign now has continued into Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you've got these forces to prosecute that with and move out today. I mean, this is -- and this happened on the 6th, you know, Operation Storm is not finished. So he is completing -- trying to finish the fight he was in, now focussed on moving forward to a larger probably unchartered territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll into evidence 65 ter 1D2934.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1635.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1635 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you referred to this to some degree before, and if we could just move to -- and I want to just talk about this briefly in the spirit of moving ahead, and if you turn to tab 15 in your binder, that's D281, the order for active defence. If you take a look at that. And is that the first step in the moving ahead?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going look at it real quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is -- it's your tab 15, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously -- I know I say obviously to anybody, but having secured the intermediate objectives, now he must posture himself for the next fight. Normally when you do that, you go into a hasty defence to allow the opportunity for you to re-set your forces, move logistics forward, and then be prepared to -- to either pass the orders and the guidance down to your subordinate units in terms of priority of work. If you think back, these -- these guys, these subordinate units have been going through some very rugged terrain, the lead effort -- the main effort of them, and he knows he has got to count on the leadership and/or those units to continue this fight. He's also got to do extensive coordination with those who are going to be on his left and right flank, and that takes a little bit of time. So that it -- allow him that time to reset those forces and/or to do adequate preparation and coordination with now moving into new territories, I mean, you're getting in specificity, like, he probably doesn't even have maps of this terrain he's been asked to go fight over. He's got to get all that out to his units, so elects, it appears, to go into a operational pause, which is a defensive-type posture, across where he -- the current forces have gained and stabilized, and that's, to me, this is the next step in preparation for his next offensive operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And while you're in this -- I just want to see if the translators have caught up. While you're in this -- this pause, or this active defence mode is one of the concerns you have a possible counterattack coming from the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, for sure. I mean, if I think about it, again, the operational forces for the total Croatian Army have been engaged. There's not another division or another large element you can bring forward, you know, to reinforce your lines with per se. So he is very thin on the -- on the frontal lines. Now, he is also -- the ratios of major combat systems which he is now, at this point in time, is confronted with when you have not only the Krajina Serbs but you have the regular Serb forces and Mladic's Operational Groups, they -- they should be able to move along those lines of communications very rapidly with their -- their combat compatibilities and focus them on a point in time, and penetrate your lines. Now whether they did that or not, is, you know, another story. But certainly at the point you went into a hasty or into a defensive posture, you've got to be very concerned, especially on the main corridors leading into your lines that a counter-offensive could happen. I think that's reinforcing the fact that Knin just fell which was a major military centre of gravity and command post for the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk with a series of maps just very briefly. I'm sorry. Let's start with a series of maps very briefly about this setting of the active defence and the counterattack by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring up a series of maps in D728.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, these are a series of maps that you reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the -- page 12 of this document. General, it's only on the screen though; it's not in your binder, so -- because we couldn't get the colour. We see the -- the lines set as of 8 August 1995 with the order of active defence being on the 9th. And if we could turn to the next map, this shows the counterattack by the Serb forces on the 12th of August, 1995. Now, what's going on here, General? What's going on in the mind of an operational commander. He sets his line, he gives the order for active defence, and lord and behold there's a counterattack several days later where he takes significant casualties. Talk to us about this.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Well, this is his worst nightmare. Obviously, when he made the turn towards Knin he exposed his flank and he did have some forces there, but his focus was back down to the south-west. And knowing that the orientation of those force would not be towards, at least with his main combat elements, not be back towards Drvar, which primarily some of the avenues approached leading into the sector were. At the same time, if you look over there at OG Ostric, I don't know how much he knew at the time, but you have a seam right there between your forces -- I'm sorry. So you are very vulnerable at the seams between two of your Operational Groups. So what's happened here is an attack right into those seams, at the same time right into your flanks of your -- of the focus of those main elements going into Knin. So that is probably the most vulnerable point and that's where obviously the enemy figured to attack, and then that would have oriented them also in retaking of Knin. So a commander right after you get ready and you go into that defensive posture has to look to see where he is vulnerable and get the forces into those areas. In this particular case, Serb forces strike within a couple of days, obviously they had some limited advantages and at the time -- but were successful in a limited manner initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just go through some of these maps quickly just to emphasise one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we go to the next map on page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the counterattack the next day by the Split Military District. Go to 15. And the settling in the lines on the 18th. And, once again, to page 16. Now, General, we have the setting of the lines, the counterattack, the retaking the ground, and then we have Operation Maestral which takes place a short time thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to the next map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: From 8 -- 8 September to 15 September. Now, General, when the setting up of the active defence and the counterattack and fighting off the counter-attack and the planning for Operation Maestral, which takes place approximately, well, 30 days or so later or less. Is all this going on at the same time, and what's the operational commander doing with these various tasks?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: If you remember back when we started earlier this morning, I talked about an offensive campaign being probably the most operationally complex that there is, this is indicative of why it is complex. You have completed taking an intermediate objective, tried to move to a -- a tactical pause in the operation, you're counterattacked, you have to mass the forces at the point of that attack, and then you must continue the fight to -- because you've achieved momentum, which you want to do, you're within the decision cycle of the opposing commander, having him now be in a reactionary mode, you want to seize that momentum and continue the fight to gain ground and gain your next objectives. So what you're seeing is that continual push forward, seizing the momentum, and achieving not only tactically but operationally strategic objectives. You can't at that time lose sight of the fight, but you must also continually prioritise your support, priorities your main effort, priorities the fires, prioritise the intelligence collection because you've got to be able to see that battlefield, and you've got to be anticipating what's going to happen next, and at the operational level that's 48/72 hours as you make those plans and give those directives their priorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's stay with that -- those priorities, for just one second, General. If I could stay with those priorities for a second -- a minute. And with General Gotovina, specifically, I mean, what are his tasking priorities given everything that's happening in this offensive operation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Well, first of all, he has got to give -- and if you look as you get into Maestral, he now has HVO and his own forces, those of which he has been accustomed to. He has got to spend some time in making sure all his subordinate commanders understand his priorities. Those who may or may not been with him, those who have now joined him, so he's got to orient those forces on where he wants them to go, give them those manoeuvre units, give them supporting fires to prosecute what he wants them to do, give them the logistic supportability, ensure that he has communications with those units, and he's got to move about the battlefield to make sure that they understand, because his presence as he continues the operations at the decisive points in this operations are probably more important than ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can move ahead in the maps to Southern Move. Just move ahead to the next one. I'm sure ... and one more map ahead where we look at the Southern Move offensive from 8 11 to October -- 8th and 11th of October of 1995. Would this continuous prioritising of tasks for General Gotovina and his subordinates continue through this October time-frame, until they achieve the results that they wanted?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Well, no doubt. I mean, my first impression is you look at Southern Move and there you have got Operational Group North. If you remember, that was the commander he relieved. So his decision back on the eve of Operation Storm must have been the right decision, because now this -- this group has become effective. So he has to continue to do that. I would say the other thing he has to do is now that he is in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he probably also has to maintain some contact with the -- his operational commanders on his left and right to make sure that he is also keeping pace and so he has another dimension because he is outside the Croatian territory to make sure that everything of which has been agreed to politically and diplomatically, as far as the use of military force, is being prosecuted and executed it based on those orders and missions. He now has also, unlike he may have had in Croatia, he has got some responsibility for his rear because he's now in -- turning over to Bosnia-Herzegovina, working in their area, so he's got to make sure that his rear area is secure. The other thing that I think he is doing, he must stay constantly engaged with the defence minister and/or the president to make sure that what is he doing is in line with their strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the last page in this sequence so we can summarise this entire operation from winter 1994 to October 1995, in terms of General Gotovina's actions as an operational commander. This is one of the maps that we viewed, General. It shows the various movements in those time-frames. Would the comments and analysis that you discussed regarding the taskings and responsibilities of General Gotovina have basically stayed constant from the winter of 1994 up in and through Southern Move in the latter part of October 1995? And I'm talking in terms of battle focus.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I think early on General Gotovina realised the responsibility he was given by his country. I think he was one of the few that also realised that his success or his failure probably dictated what would happen to the future of the country. And he also probably realised the risk that was at hand based on the forces of a combination of probably 20 per cent professional, 80 per cent conscript, which was dealt him. So his -- his focus and his battle with them, his relationships with subordinate commanders and his work with his subordinate units, those relationships were developed over time from the winter of 1994 all the way through Southern Move. I think it's his presence and his leadership, probably as it also reflected down through his subordinate commanders, and I'm -- there's probably no doubt there is some small unit leaders that really stepped up, although, obviously, not in -- part of this -- subject of this conversation, but the presence -- the leadership presence that he was able to -- to project, and the focus he gave them through his orders both verbally and written, and his ability to -- to see the battlefield and what he had to achieve and how he communicated that to his commanders, was probably exemplary. I would not have projected, from my assessment of what I read, his ability to prosecute and be the -- move his forces knowing what I knew based on reading the background of information. You know, there's other things that played into this which obviously is -- what the reaction or what the enemy did or did not do, or the lack of probably the same intestinal fortitude and focus, because they weren't fighting for their own land. They were fighting for somebody else's. Sometimes that makes a difference. But I would say in conclusion this, his focus and his ability to lead these units of to achieve this level of success was probably not predictable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I have one last area that I would like to talk to you about, and again it goes back to the paragraph 43 concerning the undisciplined behaviour and that activity not being condoned by the military or leadership at any level. And we reviewed the video on the 6th of August that we talked about, and I would like to go through a series of documents with you, and the first I'd like to discuss with you and then ask you some questions on that score --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President just to make things clear. Mr. Kehoe quoted, I think, verbatim from paragraph 43, and there -- when it comes to condoning, it says, just the last few words: "This type of activity was not to be condoned by the military or leadership at any level." Not to be condoned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you were quoting, I take it that you are grateful for Mr. Waespi to give you the accurate language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I apologise if I misread that, counsel, and I meant to read what you wrote, General, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Anyway, if we could turn to D981, and this is a day after the meeting at the Knin castle on 6th where it is talking about the fact that General Gotovina requires war booty to be registered, and he establishes a committee to register that booty and to record the matters. On the 9th, and I would tell you that there is a translation before the parties on the 9th where General Gotovina, and in the war diary, General, notes that the military police -- and you can assume this for the sake of this argument. But assume that in the war diary on the 9th, General Gotovina states that the military police must take all measures for the security of people and for the control of war booty. He also states that all law breakers, for all law breakers it is important to record via photo and video cameras and that after the completion of the tasks they will be called to the military disciplinary court. Next, I would like you to take a look at D207, an order by General Gotovina on 10 August 1995 -- excuse me 204, D204, an order by General Gotovina on 10 August 1995. It is tab 16 in your binder, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, counsel. I may have missed something, what's the source of -- you quote about military police was must take all measures of for the security of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is the e-mail that we sent you last week on the revised translation of the August 9th, 1995 entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is that in evidence already?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, we sent it to you and that's why I asked the witness to assume that that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Assuming that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct. That's why I said assume for the sake of this discussion that it says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: D204 on the 10th August 1995, General Gotovina issues this order prohibiting arbitrary movement of HV members and discusses implementing military discipline. In paragraph 2 he notes that take all necessary measures and fully engage in the implementation of the military discipline conduct and the maintenance of order in the area of responsibility and prevent arson and other illegal acts. Take resolute measures against anyone who conducts himself in an undisciplined manner. Now reviewing just these items, General, what type of effect do these types of orders or should those orders have on the subordinate commanders and the soldiers that were answerable to those subordinate commanders?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Well, what you see right now happening is the -- even though this is concurrent and at the end of Storm, it's now obviously to him that he has got to preclude or re-emphasise, first of all, to the military police what their responsibilities are. Two, he's got to direct his units to -- in such a way that would assist him and execute the responsibilities. The one piece in here which says, I think, limited movement --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's paragraph 1 of --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... to train movement and members. That means, obviously, why his people were -- in some of subordinate units, maybe not on the front lines, were arbitrarily moving about the area and he's gonna tell them to knock it off. So he's trying to help them get control in the rear. At the same time, he is re-emphasising to the military police to take action. He's telling them to document acts of indiscipline so that they can be acted on in the future. So this is another case in a series here where he's trying to make sure his forces act as a professional force not as a -- as he said back in the tape, as those who operate for war bounty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention to a couple of other exhibits, and this would be P1140, an order on 19 August 1995, and that would be tab 17 in your binder. And this was given by a commander for operative Group West, Colonel Fuzul. It notes due to the observed breakdown of order and discipline for the international reputation of Croatia, I hereby order: Establish supervision in all units and immediately take measures against the torching of buildings and killing of animals. Take disciplinary and criminal measures against responsible [sic] individuals. I think it's irresponsible individuals, excuse me. The commanders of OG West units are responsible to me for the implementation of this order. If I could turn my attention to the next tab in your binder, tab 18. Likewise, on the -- it's D884.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So based on the order of Deputy Commander of Split Military District Staff Brigadier Ademi, with the purpose of improving the control and reinforcing discipline of the Split Military District units, all commanders of the units in the zone of responsibility of operative Group West can, according to their own judgement, dismiss part of the soldiers from the units. Principally dismiss individuals or groups who are behaving in a manner that causes disturbance of discipline and order." If I can turn to the next tab in your binder, which is D885 in tab 19, General, and this is an order of the 19th of August from the commander, Major Cerina of the 134th Home Guards Brigade. "Based on the memo of the commander of operative Group West, I'm issuing the following notification: A part of the conscripts may be dismissed from the unit. Primarily dismiss the individuals in groups, who, with their behaviour, disturb the order and discipline within the unit and as such significantly impair the implementation of combat tasks. "3, it is necessary that the commanders of the units, according to their personal assessment, propose to the Manning and Staff Divisions, the names of conscripts who need to be demobilised." This last sequence of orders on the 19th, General, was on the 19th of August, 1995, and you can assume likewise that the Prosecution's expert noted, and this is on page 12847, lines 7 to 10, that: "After the 19th, the war diary reflects no further instances of learning -- of burning and looting on the territory of the Republic of Croatia by HV units."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, the last entry on burning and looting is on -- in P71, page 115 and that's on 18 August. And as I noted the transcript of Mr. Theunens's testimony was page 12842, lines 7 to 12. Excuse me, it's 12847, is that -- that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, this is a -- going from his first speech on the 6th and this the 19th. Going back to the command climate discussion that we had previously, what -- what do you conclude based on this, from the operational commander level and how it's filtering down to his -- General Gotovina's subordinates?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: What I was just thinking is, you were looking at these exhibits, this is a point in time where I think the Croatian forces have achieved their intermediate objective to re-establish and regain control of their recognised territory. At that point in time, you also see a re-emphasise -- re-emphasising by General Gotovina and/or also his subordinate commanders to get control and discipline in all areas, reinforcing the fact that they don't want -- there are soldiers who have just been part of this offensive operation, to continue to be cited as of the -- those who are doing indisciplinary acts. At the same time, I think you see during this period a -- an area where the military police and civilian police are finally able to start getting control of the areas in the rear. There is a time where they have been, and obviously following the military forces, and now it's time to reconstitute the local police stations, reconstitute the authority over the given areas now that have been liberated. So it takes a little time for that to take hold because if you remember, the military police and/or civilian police that were available to move into an area which is heavily populated with non-combatants and other personnel, not to mention the military passing through, this was a major traffic. So now you see them able to start getting control. This is also a transition period where in the offensive campaign as we start moving out of Croatia and start moving into Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, I see this as a re-emphasising and -- and putting the importance of re-establishing the security and the rule of law in the former Croatian territory into being, emphasising that down through their command. And then the other thing I see is a little bit of a transition starting to transition on demobilisation of forces that are no longer needed who may have been mobilised from all walks of life, who probably did not have the training and discipline in -- in -- early on in any case, and so it's time to have those people moved back to the communities they were called from in the first place. So I see -- I see a couple of things. Securing -- securing the area; 2, continuing the fight; 3, right-sizing the force and allowing the conscripts who were mobilised, maybe a couple of years ago or within a year ago, to go back to where they should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm looking at the clock. At the same time, asking himself how much more time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just 15 minutes, Judge, I think, and I'll be done. This is a logical place for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will have a break and -- Could I also inquire with the other Defence teams how much time they would need. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We won't have any questions for this witness, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Neither will we, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that you will start your cross-examination after the break, approximately 1.15. We will have a break and we resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, just a couple of final questions in this area, and we're talking about the issues that came up, the undisciplined conduct that came up after Operation Storm, and we looked at the orders and we looked at some of the demobilisation of problem units, et cetera. And looking at what General Gotovina did from an operational commander point of view, is there any other steps that General Gotovina should have taken that you would have taken in a similar situation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Quite frankly, at the time and with my staff, probably not. The only thing I might have done, given the opportunity in talking with the Main Staff and my bosses was to re-emphasise the point that those people who were charged with the rear operations and re-establishing the civilian control to try to get them some support because at the time I would be getting the reports, and obviously I'm not pleased about it. But at the point in time his emphasise with his commanders, and his focus being the offensive operation, I did not see a specific additional action he would have -- probably should have taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So to conclude in that area, General, do you believe that General Gotovina took all necessary and reasonable measures to address the disciplinary problems that he received notice of?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I mean, have you to -- to have to consider what he has been tasked to do and where his focus should have been and his priority of effort was the offensive. And noted he was not pleased. He told them to -- he told his subordinates to clean it up and issued orders to that effect. And I think you see them probably a little bit of laten effectiveness of his orders coming after say, 12, 14 days after the orders came out, you started to see a response, and you saw accumulation from the military police and other records that arrests were happening, disciplinary measures were taken, and so the -- he was starting the -- the theatre was -- and the country and territories that they had liberated were starting to mature then in terms of discipline and legal authority. So that's -- that was a good thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, one final question, and I would like to address your conclusory paragraph in -- in paragraph 48 of your statement. In the last sentence in paragraph 48 you note that: "In the final analysis, I do not believe that the Croatian forces would have been as successful had they had not had an operational commander such as General Gotovina directing his efforts towards accomplishing the strategic goals of the Republic of Croatia." I'd like to broad than a bit, General, and just ask you, can give the Trial Chamber an assessment of General Gotovina's overall performance, after your analysis in all aspects of the operation. Could you give the Chamber your assessment in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: First of all, let me say one of the key parts of that sentence was directing his efforts towards the accomplishment of the strategic goals of the country. He was saddled with a responsibility I think few of the other commanders understood. And I think he understood it. I think his subordinates didn't understand it all the time. I think you must look at his overall performance based on the responsibilities he was given and the focus he was given to conduct an offensive campaign which would liberate the Croatian territory and/or lead to then a more of a strategic goal of settling through the Dayton Accords a future posture of Bosnia. If you take that in that context of the operational and strategic responsibilities given to this leader, you would have to come to the conclusion that he did an admirable job. When I first looked at this, I will tell you the outcome was probably far better than I would have predicted, based on the training, the level of professionalism of his forces, and training of his leaders, and probably how they created their army as far as assimilating forces and assimilating people of different backgrounds who didn't have the experience, in terms of military service and/or didn't have the experience that you would need to go into an offensive operation. You also lacked doctrine, you also lacked a training base to continue to support your force, and when you resource your army with a number of conscripts who do not even have an oath of enlistment and therefore a commitment to what you are trying to ask them to do, I was very interested in how you overcome that risk. And obviously the way you do it is through some very courageous leadership and some focus and some leadership who understand what is at stake for their country and continues to focus ahead. So I think he did a tremendous job in executing the responsibilities given to him by his country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Jones, since the other Defence counsel have no questions for you, you will be cross-examined by Mr. Waespi. Mr. Waespi is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Waespi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me start with asking you a number of questions about the process of drafting of the report. Now, we now from D1632, the letter of the 20th of May, when the -- the formal tasking, the written tasking was given to you. Now, when you were you first approached by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I would say I was first approached in April, where I -- I met with the Defence, and they asked me about my background and my interests in being able to write a paper about the operational concept of war, the command level. So that was an introduction to the Defence and trying for them to understand my background, I think, and whether or not I had enough information or enough experience to write such a paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know why you were retained? Did -- did you know or one of the members of the Defence team know you from prior contact?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When did you start drafting your report?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I did not start drafting my report until -- as you know, I work currently for an aerospace company, and I had to go through the legal measures to make sure there is not a conflict of interest in me supporting this, and obviously their desire is to make sure that I did not support it on company time. So it was after we -- we -- I got the letter and after I clarified exactly what it is, in terms of what I thought I outlined what I thought they were asking me to do in terms of the role of the operational commander. It was at that -- it was after that time that I start sitting down and writing my paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, at that first meeting in April, do you remember what kind of information was relayed to you about what you were supposed to do, what was expected from you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Only in general. Nothing specific. That's why I asked for clarification and a paper to tell me exactly what was wanted. We basically talked about my experience, my background, where -- you know, I think from their -- from the Defence's standpoint, before they entered into any type of contract with me, they wanted to know if I could execute what they thought they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you given a deadline to complete your report?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you given a deadline to complete the -- the paper, the results of your work?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Well, initially we -- we talked about the paper, and I told them when I thought I could get it done, and they, you know, obviously told me that the trial was ongoing, and the sooner, the better, but they would allow me the time to read the documents and do the research and do it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when did you deliver your draft to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I want to say on or about ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Approximately is fine.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: About the second week of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you get any feedback from the Defence? Did they ask to you make changes, amend something?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: No. What they did do is reference for me, in terms of, This is the document you're referring to, and I would say, This is where I got the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Let me talk to you about that. What kind of documents did you receive? How many; in what form?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I received most of the documents we referred to today. I got a binder sent to me which showed -- and which a lot of it I had asked for. I asked for the task organisation. I asked for the orders and the documents, and I also got the CIA report of which led to the whole chronicle of the Bosnian campaign. I asked for some subsequent documents on -- to include the maps in the sequence of the fight and the different campaigns. I asked for the number of non-combatants which were populated in the areas and the reports of -- so I could see the actual dimensions, the terrain and area of responsibilities that we were talking about so I could actually conceive that. I asked for information on -- on -- not only the task organisations but the number of conscripts and the training that the soldiers and the leaders went through. So I got an initial, obviously, receipt of the documents you had all been using here, and then I asked for additional information so I could understand the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Approximately how many documents did you look at?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I would say somewhere in the neighbourhood of 30 different documents, and I would say that was probably in the neighbourhood of 900 to a thousand pages of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I take it you looked at documents that aren't cited in your report. You only cited a selection of them.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I looked at additional information. Obviously some of the things that were brought out today were things that I also read.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you discuss the assignment given by the Defence with anybody outside the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: No. In my agreement, I was precluded from doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you didn't discuss with any of your colleague, staff members?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: No. I'm in a civilian firm now. I'm not too sure so many of them understand what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In preparation for your report, did you ever go do Knin or the wider Knin area, the -- the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were you ever in that area before or after providing the report?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: When I was assigned to Bosnia in 1997/1998, I was -- I transited most of the areas of Bosnia to include all the way from Zagreb to Split, Sarajevo, to our sector, which was the Task Force Eagle Sector, which was largely on the western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you were in Knin at that time or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I did not physically step foot in Knin. I flew over it, and I'm familiar with the area and the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: From flying over the terrain?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not from actually being there?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: That's correct. That's by helicopter, so we're not very high.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a couple of issues about your expertise. I heard today, although I think it's not mentioned in your report or CV, that you testified in the cases following your Abu Ghraib investigation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: That's correct. I testified about my report. I testified to the department in the army, the office of the secretary of defence, obviously the secretary of defence and then to our Congress and Senate, as well as the president's Intel Select Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you ever testify in any other case?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I testified in Geneva on the compliance of the factions as far as implementing the Dayton Accords and the zone of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you ever testify in a criminal trial, whether, local, domestic, or internation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: A civilian crime trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Or military.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Of course, I have experience in military trials. In some cases, I was -- my -- may have been the presiding -- as a special court martial or military trial, and so I have military experience, mostly in terms of -- I guess you would say the special court martial level of authority, which could be felonies in that cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just seek clarification there. Are you talking about appearing as a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A witness and/or as the convening authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So two quite different capacities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Why did you convene a special court martial, if that's what you had convened? Do you remember the --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes, if it was in the purview of my authority, I would do that for a soldier who would violate the uniform code of military justice, and his offence would have required that level of -- of adjudication.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall what he did wrong?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: No, I don't recall. I mean, there's several incidents of which someone could be raised to that level of the uniform code of military justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But going back to the point I'm after, you never testified as an expert, other than today?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that is also your first expert report that you -- you drafted.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Well, if you look at it in terms of what I did in terms of Abu Ghraib, in that report, I was selected based on my experience to make an assessment of the execution and responsibilities of the commander. That was very comparable. In the military, we don't have expert witnesses as per se.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the result of that Abu Ghraib expert report was what -- in relation to -- I think you mentioned General Sanchez?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, my conclusions at that time -- I'm trying to think of whether I can state on an unclassified manner what my conclusions were. In general, my conclusions were that phase 4 of that operations [sic] were not planned adequately, and that General Sanchez was burdened with a lot of responsibilities beyond his control, and I'll leave it at that unless you want to research that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think we have it on the -- we just found the [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Yeah, I think could you find a lot of things for the unclassified sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. So Sanchez, General Sanchez was responsible yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: In -- in that instance, you know, a commander is always responsible for what happens within his command. He was not culpable and he was not negligent because of the actions he took which, very similar in this case, which he issued orders, he went down to the place and told his subordinate commanders. Plus he held his subordinate commanders responsible for anything that would happen. Some of the recommendations was to reinforce his staff with people that could oversee particularly the prisoners of war and or the interrogation process, and that happened subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did you publish anything on, you know, the subject you are testifying today, on command and control, on any other related issues?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Publish for public consumption?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, in a review, army review of the -- the air force?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Not for public domain. I have written papers in the schools about leadership, as we all have, in terms of our military education.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you left the army approximately four years ago to go into -- into commercial business?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: Three years ago. 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: In July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to now go through a number of -- of parts from your report and also your testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I first ask two clarifying questions. You talked about CIA report, and so - I'm addressing the parties - that's not in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's -- it's -- we're going to bar table. It's -- we just need to talk to counsel. It is called "Balkan Battle Grounds." It's written by the CIA. It's a public document that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We haven't seen it before --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and it's not in evidence at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you rely on any of the facts described in that CIA report? Because, if I'm not mistaken, I do not see it as a footnoted source.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it is Mr. President, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I missed --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- I'll into that. It's white --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll go into it. Yes, perhaps it is referred to by a 65 ter number. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's footnoted Judge, routinely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "Balkan Battle Grounds."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Balkan Battle Grounds." It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's it. That's the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the one, yes, yes. Then, it's clear that it's footnoted not just once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The other thing you said was that you had sources for documents given the number of non-combatants. What did you have in mind there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I asked for the -- and part of that comes out of the Balkan report. I asked for the numbers that were populated from the previous fights that had happened since 1991 and so forth, give me an estimate of how many people were -- were non-combatants in the area of Croatia, and/or the area of which was the primary responsibility of General Gotovina. That was for my understanding of what -- what had to be dealt with, to re-establish security and control in the rear area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you're talking about non-combatants of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Refugees, people with illegal crime, displaced persons, just do give me the magnitude of how many people were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, total population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Total population after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I really wanted to know what it was before and then afterwards because what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina was also an influx of refugees moving from that area, from operations that were ongoing in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so they had to go somewhere. So they were obviously migrating also into Croatia as well the other inhabitants and/or people moving throughout the areas. So I wanted a feel of what the magnitude was, displaced persons in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think I found in your report calculations on how you came to conclusion in this with respect. For example, one of the things I would be interested to know about, whether you formed any opinion about the Serb population on this Krajina-Croatian territory after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, I did not form a conclusion on a specific Serb population, whether they were there or not. What I was looking for is the number of military police, civilian police, that were allocated to re-establish the rule of law and if those were adequate. I think you will note in my report where I say sometimes we failed to plan for the post-operation, combat operations, and it requires -- just like in Iraq and the US experience or in other places, if we fail to plan for success and following the military forces to re-establish the rule of law and provide adequate resources for that, we set ourselves for failure in terms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may stop you there. What I was trying to find out is if you're talking about non-combatant population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, "I did not form a conclusion as to a specific Serb population whether they were there or not." And then you went on to see whether the number of police officers, whether military or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- civilian were adequate numbers to deal with the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if you do not know what the non-combatant Serb civilian population is, how can you establish the adequacy of police forces --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if you do not know whether the Serbs are there or are not there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not concerned about the Serbs per se. I wanted to know the total population of non-combatants in the area of operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which includes Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which includes the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Serbs would be what percentage of the whole of the non-combatant population in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't go down to that level. I went -- if you're, from a military standpoint, if you have to move through the area and you have to move your logistics through a given area which is restricted because of geography, certainly the roads and so forth are problematic because of the numbers of people trafficking on the roads and that movement of displaced persons causes, obviously, problems for military operations. So I wanted to get some kind of idea, not on specificity of how many Serbs were displaced, but how many people were in the rear areas that -- which you would -- if you were moving in to secure the area or you had to control as a military or civilian police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this seems to be two different matters. The one is how many non-combatant people are living there to police the area and this population; and you touched upon another subject which seems to me quit different. That is, to what extent is the movement of non-combatant population bothering military operations, and -- which are two quite distinct matters, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This -- two areas which are problematic but both caused by the number of non-combatants and displaced persons in an area, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For both very important to establish --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- how many there were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Actually --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wanted an idea of what was, you know, the Population of an area looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you do not know whether they were there, you wouldn't know how much they would bother you, and you wouldn't know what would be an adequate force to police them, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the other, Your Honour, the only other thing I was concerned with, if you look at the way the military operation was laid out, how did General Gotovina get his logistic support. It had to be either moved by sea, offloaded at Split and moved up, or it had to transit all the way around Croatia to come back to enable success by that envelopment that he was doing. So my first question is where did his logistics come from, and so you can imagine the difficulty of moving logistic support to his forces or moving his artillery or whatever combat forces he had to prosecute his plan. So that's -- that was just some of my thoughts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Waespi, I was only seeking the -- some further details on these two sources apparently used by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But you are exactly right. You could go into detail looking at that. I just got a general idea and moved forward.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: For the sake of the interpreters kindly don't overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes I have to apologise both to transcribers and interpreters, and I'll improve my performance. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We'll talk about these numbers, I guess, tomorrow when we discuss paragraph 36, where you talk about, I think, 700 -- the figure of 700 police officers. But let me go back actually to the observation of the Presiding Judge about the multiple entries on the -- in your footnotes about "Balkan Battle Grounds," the CIA book. I take it you relied heavily on that book in drafting your report, certainly these background parts of your report?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I would say I didn't rely as heavily as I did based on what the points were as far as the task, organisation, and military orders, but it certainly -- "Balkan Battle Grounds" reinforced a lot of the points and it was the only documented evidence I had of the -- of the larger picture of condition of forces and their estimates at the time of both the VRS and -- and -- and the Croatian forces, the readiness and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now let's look at just one entry, and I would like to go to Defence 65 ter -- actually, not even sure whether I can do that, 1D590.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if the document will be bar tabled, we have no objections to that. And perhaps it can be tendered as a whole. And it's page 18 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the size of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's fairly large.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's pretty large which is the reason why we were going to give our shaved down version to the Prosecution and come to some idea of what we jointly want together. There is a lot in this book that is of no consequence, so I thought it would be better to shave it down a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Parties are invited to agree on the relevant portions to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
