utterances.text: -- in evidence and then the Chamber will further consider it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in your report, and I want do leave this document on the screen. But in your report, in paragraph 6, you say in the middle of this paragraph, and I quote: "With respect to the Croatian Army, HV, it appears that it was created as a defence force in 1991 that was poorly trained and minimally disciplined. As a result, the institutional capabilities do not exist within the HV to act in an organised fashion until after August 1992." And then you go on to say that: "Over time the HV raised into a professional army, intensely training its troops and developing its Guards Brigades." Now, as we see from your footnote, it refers to the document we have on the screen, and it finishes your thought as contained in the report and says, and I quote from the left column, the middle of that paragraph, right above chapter 65: "And developing its Guards Brigade into the finest combat formations in the Balkans. All of this was for one purpose: The reconquest of the Republic of Serb Krajina." So, in 1995, General Gotovina had as part of his fighting force the finest fighting combinations in the Balkans. You were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I would say he didn't have the finest Guards Brigades at the time and he probably realised that. This basically says the intervening years provided an opportunity to do that, but I don't think they had developed to the finest brigades, although you could challenge the fact of all the brigades in the Balkans area, their level of training and their level of readiness compared to a professional force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you are disagreeing with the authors of this report?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: No. I think they're -- you know, what they're saying is, if you look at that -- during the intervening years, the question had raised itself on its own bootstraps, you know, and so forth, and it was developing its guards brigades into what they envisioned to be the finest combat formations in the Balkans. They had not achieved that in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, you are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I ask you, just looking at the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the text in view of, you say they had an opportunity to do so, but they didn't do it; or does the text say that is what they did? Just -- because, we have to clearly find out where your opinion as to what the standard to which it finally developed is, and what this report says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it seemed to me that you started answering that the document would say that the intervening years provided an opportunity to do that but you don't think they had done it. Whereas, although not being a native English-speaking person, I get the impression that the text, true or not, tells us that they did take that opportunity and that they developed the Guards Brigades into the finest combat formations into the Balkans. Again, whether true or not, but I'm just trying to find out whether we read the text in a very different way or that it is that you disagree with what is written here, which are two different --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this particular case, the level of maturity at which they have done that, I disagree with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their statement of that perspective at the time, the [indiscernible] was read in 2002, it may have been from a perspective of where they started to where they achieved, was developing those brigades into one of the finest brigades in the Balkans at the time in 1995. I will tell you, just as General Gotovina said in February 1995, he still lacked non-commissioned officers. He still lacked junior level leadership. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you will not mind, I'll interrupt you because my question was exclusively and primarily focusing on the following.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it that we read something entirely different in the same text or is it just that you disagree what is written here and I want to clearly distinguish between the two options and I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that is clear to me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you disagree with what is written here as a result of what happened between 1991 and the later stages. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go on the same page, left column to the bottom and look at another aspect, a similar one. Last two lines talks about General Bobetko, who was the commander in chief of -- chief of the HV Main Staff from November 1992 onwards, and it says: "Bobetko's appointment confirmed that preparing the HV to retake the Krajina from the Serbs would be the army's unifying mission. He moved quickly to halt the demobilisation, create additional Guards Brigades and shuffle the officers serving on the Main Staff, the corps commanders, and the Guards Brigades. Bobetko appointed officers loyal to him and his objective, forming a team that would develop a HV way of doing business in doctrine, training, and attitude." Do you agree with me that, at least according to this report, already from 1991/1992, they were preparing for actions in the Krajina, whenever that's going to -- to be taking place?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: My interpretation of this is: As I look at General Bobetko and what he was trying to do, he probably realised the fact that they did not have a professional army, no matter the mission in the future would be. He was probably one of the earlier general officers that saw the need for training, an institutional training base, and he was trying to get people who realised that -- that need, to help him put that together. And I think his initial efforts towards writing doctrine was the right thing to do if, in fact, he was going to have a professional force. I don't see that a direct correlation to the Krajina or the other particular mission at hand we saw in the winter of 1994 and so sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So can you disagree that everything what the HV did according to plans by General Bobetko both focusing on to retake the Krajina. You would disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: I would disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY JONES
utterances.text: At that point in time, he had no way of having the insider capability of doing that because they were trying to create a force completely and defence would have been the first mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't say he already had the capability at that time. What's in the report was working towards that, ending up with the [indiscernible] brigades in the Balkans, but we have discussed that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I can tender this document for transparency purpose or we can do it altogether. I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that the parties sit together to see what portions of this document will be used and that the relevant portions with sufficient context will be tendered. Mr. Waespi, I'm also looking at the clock and since I have two minor procedural matters, I wonder whether this would be an appropriate time to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- stop. But before doing so, Mr. Jones, first I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone, whomever about your testimony, whether the testimony that you have given already today or the testimony still to follow tomorrow. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00, although in a different courtroom. It will be Courtroom III. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Jones out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the record, we do understand that Mr. Markac wants to waive his right to be present in court on the 4th of September. That's put on the record. The message was rather short. I take it that will be for personal reasons and that we do not have to explore in any further detail. That's on the record. Second, the Chamber was still informed that there were still some questions about a non-proofing of guidance of 92 bis witnesses. The Chamber also understood that the Defence might have some problems with that if cross-examination would deal with matters, other than what one would primarily expect it to do with. Of course, the Chamber is not in a position to give any further guidance, not knowing what areas will be covered in cross-examination; so, therefore, I don't know whether there has been an exchange of views or whether it has been inquired already by the Defence, whether the Prosecution would want to cover areas which the Defence considers such that it would need to proof the witness. Has such a communication taken place?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It has not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps that is the logical first step to take. And if then any problem remains, Mr. Russo, then, of course, the Chamber will hear from you again. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do intend do go into matters pursuant to our obligations under 90(H). However, since the Defence doesn't know what those areas will be, it seems to me that there 's no connection between what we may go into and what they can proof the witness on so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see. Your obligations under 90(H), but correct me whether I'm wrong - I was not raised in a common law environment - your obligations arise once you have established that there -- the witness has knowledge on matters which would support your case and then you have certain duties. Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I think respect to matters with which the witness is competent to testify, if he testifies contrary to the Prosecution's case then we're required to put the nature of our case to him. The other obligations of seeking to elicit evidence from him which may support our case is permissive and not obligatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the primary purpose still being to establish the presence of, I would say, the witness and another witness who has testified in this court at certain moments, at certain places. That's still the primary focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just so I can put our position on the record. If he testifies in direct in a manner that -- in direct, which I don't think there is going to be a direct that's contrary to their position, and it's already in the statements, then the Prosecution already knows whether they intend to go beyond the issue for which the witness has been called. From our position, if that is in fact the case, there is no need or reason that we should be precluded from proofing a witness, because as the Chamber knows and the case law is clear, we also have the opportunity to test the credibility of our witnesses on any matter. And if we were to find in proofing that there was a lack of credibility, we can always withdraw the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still seems to be something to be discussed by the parties whether serious address should be made to the Chamber, whether or not to change the guidance given until now. The Chamber, at this very moment, remains passive, expects the parties to -- to exchange their views on what exactly Rule 90(H) requires them to do and what one could expect in cross-examination, the witnesses being 92 bis witnesses and not 92 ter witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will have to check the Rules, but that was an additional question I had, Mr. President, is that under 92 bis, I must confess, I haven't looked it up yet, but whether cross-examination is allowed under 92 bis and if not, does that mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it becomes 92 ter. I do agree, but what I wanted to express, although not very clearly, is that we expect these witnesses to be cross-examined briefly on the matters which we find in the 92 bis or 92 ter statement. We then will adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, the 1st of September, 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of September, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
